raw.answer: Taiwan's pharmacists' law said a licensed pharmacist could practice at only one location. Several pharmacists and a judge challenged this, along with a health authority letter requiring people who are both pharmacists and nurses to work at one place. The court held the one-location rule unconstitutional because it had no reasonable exceptions, and held the letter invalid because it added a restriction that no law provided.
raw.held: Article 11 of the Pharmacists Act (one practice location only) violates the proportionality principle and the right to work, and loses effect at the latest one year after the ruling. The 2011 letter limiting dual pharmacist-nurse practitioners to one location violates the principle of legal reservation and may no longer be applied.

points.text: Limits on how and where people work are allowed only to serve the public interest and only if the means are truly necessary, under the proportionality principle.

The one-location rule aims to support full-time pharmacists, prevent license renting, protect the medicine management system and allocate health workers well; the purpose is legitimate but the limit must not go beyond what is necessary.

Pharmacists do different kinds of work, and helping out at free clinics, remote or disaster areas, and care homes does not conflict with the law's purpose. The authorities already allowed such cases flexibly, so exceptions are needed. A flat ban with no reasonable exceptions is an unnecessary restriction and conflicts with the right to work. Revision is due within one year.
The different treatment of pharmacists and other health professionals did not breach the equality principle, because the legislature may set different rules given differences in the professions.

Rules limiting where people with several health qualifications may practice affect job freedom and public health, so they must be set by law or by a clearly authorized order. The Pharmacists Act has no such rule, so the letter added a restriction without legal basis.
Other challenged provisions were not accepted for review because the applicants did not explain specifically how they violated the constitution.

who: People qualified as both pharmacist and nurse
Pharmacies and medical institutions needing pharmacist help

raw.answer: The case concerned a 2010 Ministry of National Defense recruitment notice for reserve officer and reserve noncommissioned officer classes, which barred anyone who had ever received a criminal sentence from applying. The court held that the rule had a proper legal basis, but that it went too far because it also shut out people with minor, one-off negligent offences. The relevant agencies must draft future notices for similar exams in line with this ruling.
raw.held: The ban on applicants with any criminal sentence does not violate the rule that restrictions need a legal basis. However, it exceeds what is necessary, breaches the proportionality principle, and conflicts with the constitutional right to hold public office.

points.text: Serving as a reserve officer or noncommissioned officer is a public office, and the exam is the necessary gateway to it, so barring people from the exam restricts their right to hold public office.
The rule has a legal basis: legislation authorized the Ministry of National Defense to set selection and admission rules, and the notice stayed within that authorization.
Authorities may limit exam eligibility to select suitable people, but any limit must still meet the proportionality principle.
The goal is legitimate and the means help achieve it: reserve officers may hold weapons and use force, so character and ability matter for military strength and security.

Excluding people convicted of intentional crimes, or negligent ones, is generally necessary. But a negligent offender who offended once and only slightly cannot be assumed to lack the character or ability for service.
Denying such people the chance to take the exam is not the least harmful way to reach the goal, so it goes beyond what is necessary.

who: People with a past criminal sentence who want to apply to be reserve officers or noncommissioned officers
People convicted of minor, one-off negligent offences
Ministry of National Defense and related agencies drafting recruitment notices

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of the Interior rule is constitutional when it says that the directors and supervisors of a civic organization immediately lose their powers once the authorities order the organization to be put in order within a time limit. The court decided that this part of the rule is unconstitutional because no law clearly authorized it. The part stops being valid at the latest one year after the ruling is announced.
raw.held: The part of Article 20, paragraph 1 of the 2006 Implementation Rules for Supervising Civic Organizations that suspends directors' and supervisors' powers at once when an organization is ordered to reorganize violates the legal-reservation principle in Article 23 of the Constitution. It infringes freedom of association and the right to work, and loses effect at the latest one year after the ruling is announced.

points.text: Freedom of association protects both individuals and the associations themselves, including their formation, continuation and activities, and the right to work covers freedom to pursue an occupation whether for public or private benefit, profit or non-profit.

Choosing directors and supervisors and their carrying out of duties affects how an association operates, its members' aims, and the directors' and supervisors' own occupational freedom. Limiting these freedoms must be done by law or by an order the legislature has clearly authorized, under the legal-reservation principle.

Ordering a time-limited reorganization under the Civic Organizations Act, Article 58, paragraph 1 affects freedom of association and directors' and supervisors' right to work. Its procedures and legal effects must therefore be set by law or by an order the legislature clearly authorized.

The rule's immediate suspension of directors' and supervisors' powers restricts these freedoms but lacks a clear legal authorization, so it violates the legal-reservation principle and infringes the freedoms in Articles 14 and 15.

The court also noted that professional organizations have compulsory membership but are generally not given public power, and are under stronger supervision. It said the authorities should carefully adjust their functions and the level of supervision, and build suitable rules.

who: Directors and supervisors of civic organizations

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Ministry of Education's pay-scale rules for teachers in public schools up to senior high level were valid, since no law or clearly authorized regulation set teacher pay. The court decided the rules violate the constitutional principle that important matters need a statutory basis. The rules lose effect after at most three years unless a law is made.
raw.held: The 2004 version of the Public School Staff Salary Rules, as applied to teachers in public schools at senior high level and below, violates the constitutional principle of legal reservation. It stops being effective at the latest three years after the ruling is announced.

points.text: Under the legal reservation principle, government measures involving major public interest or protection of basic rights need a law or a clearly authorized law as their basis, even if they do not restrict freedoms.
Teacher pay, including salary calculation, affects teachers' livelihood, their property rights, and the public interest, so it must be set by law or a clearly authorized regulation.
No law currently sets teacher salary placement, and laws that say pay should be set by law have not led to a pay statute being made, so the interim rules have lasted too long.

The rules cover salary grades, amounts, calculation standards and re-grading after further study, which affect teachers' income, yet they have no statutory authorization, so they violate the principle.
The petitioner challenged only one note in the rules, but that note is part of the rules, so the court could review the whole set of rules.
Because a pay system needs time to plan, the relevant authorities have three years to make a teacher pay law, and if not done, the rules lapse for these teachers.

who: Public school teachers at senior high level and below
Authorities responsible for making a teacher pay law

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule is constitutional that makes courts refuse to approve an adoption of a mainland Chinese person when the Taiwan adopter already has a child or adopted child. The court held that, as applied to someone adopting their spouse's mainland-resident child, the rule goes too far and is unconstitutional. That part stops having effect from the day the ruling was announced.
raw.held: The part of Article 65, item 1, of the Taiwan-Mainland relations statute that makes courts refuse to approve a Taiwan resident's adoption of their spouse's mainland child is inconsistent with the constitution's protection of the freedom to adopt (Article 22) and the proportionality principle (Article 23). It loses effect from the day of the ruling.

points.text: The freedom to adopt is protected by Article 22 because adoption is part of the family system and matters for the personal development of both adopter and adopted child.
The rule limits the freedom of Taiwan residents to adopt mainland residents, and the constitution allows special legislation on relations between the two sides.
Courts should respect the legislature on cross-strait matters unless there is an obvious serious flaw, but any limit on this freedom must still meet the proportionality principle.
The rule's aim of protecting Taiwan's security and social stability by avoiding population imbalance is legitimate, and the rule helps achieve it.
Adopting a spouse's mainland child supports marital happiness, family harmony and the child's development, yet the rule makes no exception for it.
So the harm to this freedom is out of balance with the public interest protected, making the limit excessive.

who: Taiwan residents who want to adopt a spouse's mainland child
Mainland-resident children of spouses of Taiwan residents
Taiwan residents who already have children or adopted children

raw.answer: The case asked whether the income tax law is unconstitutional because it lets people deduct medical bills only if paid to certain listed hospitals and clinics, even for people who need long-term care because they cannot look after themselves. The court decided that, for these long-term care patients, the rule breaches the constitutional guarantee of equality. In that scope the rule may not be applied.
raw.held: The income tax rule limiting itemized medical-expense deductions to payments made to the listed hospitals and clinics is inconsistent with the equality principle in Article 7 of the Constitution as applied to long-term care patients, and in that scope it must not be applied.

points.text: Equality is judged by whether the purpose of the different treatment is constitutional and whether the classification is connected to that purpose.
The rule creates different treatment depending on which clinic or hospital a person used, and the court limited its review to the part concerning long-term care patients.

Because the rule affects the survival rights of long-term care patients, who may have to use other lawful providers owing to how medical resources and facilities are distributed, the court applied stricter review requiring a substantial connection between the means and the purpose.

The aim of preventing abuse and tax avoidance and easing tax authorities' checking is acknowledged, but long-term care costs are necessary to sustain life and should be deductible whichever lawful provider is paid.

Tax authorities can still review whether an expense is a real medical expense, so administrative cost would not rise much, and the rule's effect on preventing abuse is not significant while its burden on patients is heavy.
So the different treatment lacks a substantial connection to its purpose and does not fit the equality principle.

raw.answer: The case asked whether 2006 rules that capped how much of their lump-sum old-age insurance payout retired civil servants and school staff could put in a preferential-interest deposit were unconstitutional. The Constitutional Court ruled they were not: they do not apply law retroactively, and they do not violate the protection of reasonable reliance or the proportionality principle. It also said the authorities should avoid cutting retirees' income to a level that harms their dignity.
raw.held: The rules that reduce the amount eligible for preferential-interest deposits, by capping monthly retirement income at a percentage of the pay of the same grade still in service, do not involve forbidden retroactive application. Although affected people had protectable reliance, the measures did not go beyond what is necessary and reasonable, so they do not violate reliance protection or proportionality.

points.text: The rules apply only to legal relationships that continue after they took effect, not to matters already concluded, and deposits already contracted for a term were not subject to them, so they are not forbidden retroactive law.

Reliance protection means that when a law without a set end date is changed, the change needs a public-interest reason and must be weighed against the reliance interest, avoiding total termination and considering phasing and differing ability to bear the cut.
The deposit scheme had no end date and ran for a long time, and retirees and serving staff built it into their planning, so their reliance deserves constitutional protection.

The change served a public interest: over three decades conditions changed greatly, the new pension system left some retirees with unreasonably high income, and the interest cost burdened state finances and crowded out other spending.
The measure was moderate: it did not abolish the deposits abruptly but set an income-replacement cap that reflects differing grades, so it did not exceed what is necessary and reasonable.
The rules apply only to those with both old and new system service who draw or will draw monthly pensions, not to lump-sum recipients or those with only one system's service.

who: Retired civil servants and school staff drawing monthly pensions
Serving civil servants and school staff expecting such pensions

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's legislative election system is unconstitutional. That system combines single-seat districts with party-list seats under two separate votes, and it requires a party to win 5% of the party vote to get list seats. The court decided these rules do not violate the free and democratic constitutional order, and it declined to hear parts of two petitioners' requests.
raw.held: The constitutional amendment provisions on the two-vote parallel system, the party-list seats and the 5% party threshold do not violate the free and democratic constitutional order. The matching provision in the Public Officials Election and Recall Act raises no constitutional doubt. The court did not accept the petitions of one petitioner on the district-seat rule and of the Green Party.

points.text: Amendments to the constitution deserve respect unless the procedure is clearly and seriously flawed or the content violates the free and democratic constitutional order. That order rests on the democratic republic principle, popular sovereignty, protection of people's rights, and separation and balance of powers.
The amendments set up a two-vote system: single-seat districts for regional seats and party-list voting for the 34 national and overseas seats. The two kinds of seats are counted separately.

Electoral methods may not obstruct the democratic republic or popular sovereignty principles, nor change the core of the right to vote and equality. Within those limits, the amending body has room to weigh and choose.

The mixed design balances district representation with party diversity and reflects the people's will. It does not conflict with those principles, and it cannot be faulted by comparison with other systems such as the linked (聯立) system.

The 5% threshold may make votes count unequally, but it aims to prevent many tiny parties from fragmenting the legislature and hindering its work. Parties other than the two big ones are not wholly shut out, so the core of voting and equality rights is unchanged.
The election act provision on the parallel system and threshold was made under the amendment and has the same content, so it raises no constitutional doubt.

The court did not accept one petitioner's challenge to the rule of at least one seat per county or city, because it concerns district seats, not party-list elections, and no harm to its rights was explained. It also did not accept the Green Party's petition, because the party was only a participant in the final judgment, not a party to it.

who: Petitioners Constitution-Making Alliance and Green Party

raw.answer: The case was about the rules for landowners who organize their own urban land readjustment (self-run projects that regroup land in an area). The court found that several parts of the Incentive Measures were unconstitutional because they lacked fair administrative procedures or went beyond what the law allowed. It found that the approval ratio set in Article 58, paragraph 3 of the Equalization of Land Rights Act could not simply be called a violation of proportionality or equality.
raw.held: The rules on who may apply to set up a preparatory committee, on handing the committee powers that belong to the readjustment association, and on how authorities approve the project scope and plan violate the Constitution. Relevant authorities must fix them within one year, or those parts lose effect; the consent ratio in Article 58, paragraph 3 was not held to violate proportionality or equality.

points.text: Self-run readjustment can restrict the property rights and residential freedom of owners who do not agree, so each step must follow constitutionally required fair administrative procedure.

The rule on applying to set up the committee sets no minimum share of land area, and for seven or more initiators no share of owners. A few owners could therefore force many others, or owners with more land, into the project, which is not substantively fair.

Applying for approval of the project scope, and for approval and announcement of the plan, are powers of the readjustment association. Giving them to the preparatory committee conflicts with the Act and exceeds its delegation, violating the legal reservation principle.

Approving the scope and the plan are administrative dispositions that restrict rights. The rules do not require a suitable review body, a chance to be heard, delivery to other owners, or a public hearing with reasons, so they fall short of fair procedure.
The unconstitutional parts of the Measures must be reviewed and revised within one year of the ruling's announcement, or they lose effect.

The consent ratio in the Act is a matter for the legislature unless it is too low to meet fair procedure. Using the same ratio as another article, or not varying it by type, does not clearly violate proportionality or equality, though authorities are urged to review it.

who: Landowners in proposed readjustment areas who do not agree
Landowners who agree to take part
Holders of other rights over the land

raw.answer: The case arose from the Taipei City Government's use of land expropriated for a metro depot in a joint development project, where the land was developed with private parties and sold on. The court held that land expropriated for a metro system under Article 6 of the Mass Rapid Transit Act cannot be used for a joint development under Article 7 in the same plan. Transferring such land to third parties also needs a clear statutory basis.
raw.held: Authorities may not use land expropriated under Article 6 of the Mass Rapid Transit Act for a joint development approved under Article 7(1) in the same plan. Expropriated land may be transferred to a third party only if a law clearly allows it, to protect property rights under the Constitution.

points.text: The Control Yuan and the Executive Yuan disagreed on whether the two provisions could be used together and whether expropriated land could be transferred to private owners under joint development, so the request for a unified interpretation was accepted.

Article 6 expropriation serves the specific purpose of building the metro system, not commercial gain, while Article 7 joint development aims at using land efficiently and involves sharing commercial profit and risk.

Because the expropriation was for the metro purpose, the authority cannot use that land for joint development in the same plan or transfer its ownership to third parties; if circumstances change, a later plan must follow the laws then in force.
Matters affecting public interest or basic rights must be set by law, and any delegation must be specific and clear.

Transferring expropriated property to a third party risks abuse of the expropriation power and doubts about favoring particular parties, so a later joint development requires a law clearly allowing the transfer.

who: People whose land is expropriated for metro projects
Private joint development partners and buyers

raw.answer: Two petitioners, the Taipei City Government and Chi Chia-wei, asked the Constitutional Court whether Taiwan's Civil Code marriage chapter is unconstitutional because it does not let two people of the same sex marry. The court decided that it is: leaving them out violates the constitutional guarantee of freedom of marriage and the guarantee of equality. It gave the legislature two years to fix the law.
raw.held: The marriage provisions of the Civil Code, to the extent they do not let two people of the same sex form an intimate, exclusive and permanent union for the purpose of a shared life, violate the constitution's marriage freedom (Article 22) and equality (Article 7). The relevant authorities must amend or enact laws within 2 years; if they do not, same-sex couples may register marriage under the marriage chapter with a written document signed by at least two witnesses.

points.text: The court agreed to decide because the issue is highly contested, the legislature has not finished legislating after more than ten years, and fundamental rights are at stake.

Earlier rulings mentioning one man and one woman were made in the context of heterosexual marriage, and the court had never ruled on whether same-sex couples may marry. The current marriage chapter is read as covering only a man and a woman.

Freedom to marry, including whom to marry, is a fundamental right protected by Article 22. Same-sex marriage would not affect existing opposite-sex marriages or the social order, and the need for such a union is the same for same-sex and opposite-sex people. Leaving it out is a serious legislative defect.

The marriage chapter treats people differently by sexual orientation, a hard-to-change trait, and same-sex people have long faced discrimination and are a politically weak minority. So a stricter equality test applies.

Neither procreation nor protecting basic ethical order justifies excluding same-sex couples. The law does not require fertility for marriage, and allowing same-sex marriage would not disturb the ethical order. The exclusion therefore breaches equality.

Because the matter is complex, the legislature gets two years and may choose the form, such as amending the marriage chapter or creating a special law. If it misses the deadline, same-sex couples may register marriage directly, with spousal rights and duties.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a government rule setting a 2-year deadline for health care providers to submit National Health Insurance service points for payment was constitutional. The court held that the rule was unconstitutional because a deadline of this kind that cuts off a legal claim must be set by statute, not by an administrative regulation. The rule therefore may not be applied.
raw.held: Article 6, paragraph 1 of the 2000 review measures, which said the insurer must not pay points claimed more than two years past the filing deadline, violates the legal reservation principle and infringes property rights, so it must not be applied. The request for a provisional order was rejected because the ruling made one unnecessary.

points.text: Limitation periods serve stability of legal order and affect public interest and people's rights and duties, so for both public and private law claims they must be set directly by statute, not by regulation.
The National Health Insurance Act as enacted set no deadline for providers to submit service points; the 2-year limit came only from the regulation issued by the authority.
Submitting points is exercising a public law claim with property value, so the deadline works as a limitation period for that claim.
Setting that limitation period by regulation added a restriction the law did not contain, violating the legal reservation principle and property rights under Articles 15 and 23 of the Constitution.
A provisional order was unnecessary because the court had already ruled on the case itself.

who: The authority that issues the review regulations

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional that a business which operated without registering cannot use purchase receipts first produced after being caught to offset its sales tax when the tax shortfall is calculated. The court held that the Ministry of Finance's 2000 letter setting this rule does not conflict with the constitutional principle that taxes must be set by law. Separately, some parts of the petitions were not accepted for review.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 2000 letter, which bars offsetting sales tax with input receipts first produced after the business was caught, fits the purpose of the relevant business tax provisions and does not violate Article 19 of the Constitution.

points.text: Article 19 requires the main elements of a tax to be set by law, but technical and detailed matters may be explained by administrative orders, so long as the explanation fits the law's purpose, the tax's economic meaning and fair substantive taxation.
The earlier Interpretation No. 660 already upheld the same letter as applied to Article 51, item 3; the item 1 part at issue here was not covered and so had to be decided now.

Under the value-added tax rules, input tax can be deducted only if the business holds a lawful receipt and files it within the filing period; input tax first produced after being caught does not meet this requirement.

The letter's rule fits the periodic, self-checking design of the tax and the idea that businesses meeting their duties can pass tax on to consumers; it also avoids treating non-compliant businesses like compliant ones, which would undermine the registration and filing system.
Because the letter only applies the existing rules to calculate the shortfall and the fine, it adds no new legal duty and does not conflict with the principle that taxes be set by law.

A petitioner's complaint about Article 33 was not specific enough, and a Ministry letter replying to an individual case is not a law or regulation that can be challenged, so those parts were not accepted.

who: Businesses that register and file on time
Petitioners whose claims were not accepted

raw.answer: The case concerned military judges who entered service voluntarily through a special exam and had not yet been approved to serve to the maximum age or term. To stay on, they had to apply to remain, and if refused they were released from service. The court held that applying these rules to such judges conflicts with judicial independence and the right to a court hearing, and that the rules must stop applying to them within two years.
raw.held: The approval procedure for staying on and the release-at-end-of-term rule may not be applied to these military judges, at the latest two years after the ruling. The relevant authorities must amend the law within that time to set selection standards and fair legal procedures for these judges.

points.text: Military trial bodies exercise the state's power to punish, which is a judicial power, so they must follow minimum fair-process requirements and the constitutional principles of how courts are set up.

Like judges, military judges need job protection different from ordinary officers, so they can rule independently and soldiers tried before them get an independent, fair hearing. They may not be dismissed, suspended, transferred or have pay cut except for specified reasons and through fair procedure.
Under the rules, officers not yet approved to serve to the maximum age or term must apply to stay on, and those refused are released from service and removed from their officer post.
These rules apply to military judges without any special consideration for their position as judges, and whether a judge can keep judging depends on a superior's approval of the application.

The approval decision lacked fair procedures, such as an impartial committee and a chance for the judge to respond. Its selection standards could also end a judge's service without a criminal or disciplinary penalty or a properly reviewed finding of unfitness, so their status is not secured.

The petitioner's separate challenge to other provisions was dismissed because it only disputed how the courts applied the law and did not specifically show how those provisions violate the Constitution.

who: Military judges who entered service voluntarily via the special exam
Military judges not yet approved to serve to the maximum age or term
Authorities that must amend the law

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule requiring government contractors with more than 100 employees in Taiwan to hire a set share of Indigenous people, or pay a fee if they do not, is unconstitutional. The court decided the rule does not violate the constitution's equality principle, its proportionality principle, or its protection of property and freedom to do business. It also told the authorities to review and improve the rules promptly.
raw.held: The rules requiring winning government bidders with more than 100 domestic employees to hire Indigenous people for at least 1% of staff, or else pay into the Indigenous employment fund, are constitutional. They do not breach the equality principle, the proportionality principle, or the protection of property and business freedom.

points.text: The rule limits contractors' business freedom and property, so it must meet the equality and proportionality principles.

Its purpose is legitimate: it carries out the constitution's commitment to protect and support Indigenous peoples, by promoting their employment and improving their economic and social conditions, in line with international standards.

The burden is not excessive: government procurement involves public funds, the quota is only 1%, and a firm that does not hire can pay a fee based on monthly minimum wage, which it can assess before bidding.
The fee goes to the Indigenous employment fund to promote their employment, so the limit on contractors' property is not clearly out of balance with the public interest.

Treating firms over 100 employees differently is reasonable because larger firms are more flexible in hiring and better able to share the state's duty. Indigenous people are generally at a competitive disadvantage in the job market.

The measure mostly provides short-term or low-skill jobs, so the state must do more, review the measure regularly, and consider reducing fees that exceed the contract amount. Relevant authorities should review the laws promptly.

who: Government contractors with over 100 domestic employees
Government authorities that must review the rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Assembly and Parade Act is unconstitutional because it requires permission for outdoor assemblies even when they are urgent or spontaneous. The court decided that these requirements go too far and unnecessarily restrict the freedom of assembly. The provisions lose effect from 1 January 2015 (year 104 of the Republic of China calendar).
raw.held: The requirement to apply for permission for outdoor assemblies and parades, to the extent it does not exempt urgent and spontaneous ones, and the related urgent-assembly permission rules in Articles 9(1) proviso and 12(2), violate the proportionality principle and the freedom of assembly. They become invalid from 1 January 2015, and Interpretation No. 445 is supplemented.

points.text: Freedom of assembly lets people peacefully express views and influence public opinion and policy, so any legal limit must meet the proportionality principle.

Outdoor assemblies affect public order and use public resources, so lawmakers may require advance permission or notice so authorities can plan, and Interpretation No. 445 accepted permission as the general rule.
Urgent assemblies cannot realistically wait for permission, and spontaneous ones have no organizer who could apply beforehand.

The rules for urgent assemblies only relax the deadline; people must still apply and wait up to 24 hours, and spontaneous assemblies still need permission. This imposes a duty that is hard to follow, with immediate consequences such as forced stops or orders to disperse.
This conflicts with Interpretation No. 445, which said assembly freedom does not exclude spontaneous assemblies and that permission has no place for them.
Lawmakers could use less harmful means than permission to keep order, so the restriction is unnecessary and violates proportionality.

who: People holding urgent assemblies or parades

raw.answer: Foundation-run hospitals that wanted to keep their income-tax exemption could choose to book the full cost of medical buildings and equipment as a capital expense in the year of purchase. A Ministry of Finance tax bureau ruling then barred them from claiming depreciation in later years. The court held this part of the ruling unconstitutional because it changed the tax base set by law without legal authority.
raw.held: The parts of the 1995 Ministry of Finance tax bureau resolutions that required full capital-expense treatment to be deducted from non-sales income, and that barred depreciation in later years, violate Article 19 of the Constitution (tax must be set by law). They may no longer be applied from the date of the interpretation.

points.text: The court accepted the petition on resolution 3, including one lower court judgment that applied it in substance without saying so. It also reviewed the closely related part of resolution 1.
Article 19 requires the elements of a tax to be set by law. An agency's reading of a law may not go beyond it or add tax burdens the law does not impose.

Under the Income Tax Act, income is taxed after deducting costs. Fixed assets lasting two years or more are recognized as costs through yearly depreciation, and costs should be recognized according to what they actually relate to.
Under the resolutions, a hospital choosing full capital-expense treatment deducted the cost from non-sales income and could not deduct it yearly from sales income.

Even if a hospital meets the exemption standard, it must still compute its sales income with yearly depreciation. Denying that deduction conflicts with the Income Tax Act and changes the tax base by regulation, violating Article 19.

For fairness, an asset's cost that is depreciated against sales income cannot also be deducted in full against non-sales income. The court also asked the authorities to review the spending-ratio rule, which affects tax fairness and competitive neutrality between hospitals.

who: Foundation-run hospitals and their affiliated hospital organizations

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is constitutional to require a business that buys goods at a court auction to use only the tax payment slip (deduction copy) issued by the tax authority, not the seller, as its input tax document. The court held that the rules imposing this requirement violate the constitutional principle that taxes must rest on law (Article 19), and they may no longer be applied. It also said the Ministry of Finance should approve court-issued receipts as valid input tax documents.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1988 implementation notes (item 6) and its 1996 letter, which limit input tax documents for court auctions to the tax authority's payment slip deduction copy, violate Article 19's rule that taxes must be set by law, and are not to be applied.

points.text: Article 19 requires tax duties and breaks to be set by law or a clearly authorized order. Agencies interpreting tax law must follow the law's purpose and may not add tax burdens the law does not contain.

Under the business tax law, a seller issues a voucher showing the tax. The buying business can use it to deduct input tax from its output tax, whether or not the seller has paid the tax. The Ministry of Finance is authorized to approve other vouchers issued by the seller.

In a court auction the court stands in the seller's place, and the price includes business tax. The proceedings are strict, the court's receipt is credible, the tax amount can be calculated by formula, and court records can prove the details. So the court's receipt is equivalent to a seller's voucher.

The challenged rules require the tax authority's payment slip and make it depend on the tax being collected. This excludes the court's receipt and conflicts with the law's provisions on seller-issued vouchers and the Ministry's approval power.

As a result, buyers cannot deduct the input tax passed on to them in the auction price, which adds a tax burden the law does not contain and is inconsistent with the principle that taxes must rest on law.
Relevant agencies should consult quickly, and the Ministry of Finance should approve court receipts that state the goods and the price, or attach auction records showing them, as input tax vouchers.

who: Businesses that buy goods at court auctions

raw.answer: Civil courts and an administrative court had reached different views on whether the contract between an insurance agent and the insurance company counts as a labor contract under the Labor Standards Act. The court decided there is no automatic answer: it depends on how much control the agent has over how and when the work is done and whether the agent bears the business risk. It also said the agents' administrative management rules cannot by themselves settle the question.
raw.held: Whether an insurance agent's solicitation contract is a labor contract depends on whether the agent can freely decide how the work is done (including working time) and bears the business risk, for example being paid based on premiums collected. The agents' management rules cannot be used alone to decide it.

points.text: The courts disagreed: the administrative court stressed the company's supervisory power and protecting workers, while the civil courts stressed the agent's freedom and risk, so a unified interpretation was warranted.

The Labor Standards Act does not define a labor contract or employment relationship, and paid work contracts are not all labor contracts, so the nature of the work must be examined case by case, including supervision over time, place or expertise and who bears business risk.

Agents and companies may choose a contract form such as employment, mandate, contracting or brokerage, and whether it is a labor contract depends on the degree of subordination in the whole contract and facts.

If an agent freely decides the soliciting work and hours, has no base salary or required performance level and bears the business risk, subordination is low and it is hard to call it a labor contract, even if the agent can sell only that company's policies.
The agent management rules are administrative regulations made to manage agents' solicitation conduct and do not fix the type of relationship, so they cannot be the sole basis for deciding.
Parts of the petition challenging other provisions were not accepted because some were not applied in the final judgments and the rest did not specifically show any conflict with the Constitution.

raw.answer: The Legislative Yuan asked the Supreme Prosecutors Office for investigation files while reviewing amendments to a communications surveillance law, and the office refused. The court decided that the Legislative Yuan may not obtain files on ongoing investigations, but may obtain files on closed cases under strict conditions.
raw.held: The Legislative Yuan may not call up files in cases still under investigation. For cases closed without indictment or otherwise concluded, it may do so only for a clearly defined bill closely tied to its constitutional powers, where no law forbids it, and any information obtained must be used only as needed for those powers while protecting people's rights.

points.text: The Legislative Yuan's power to demand reference materials and documents only supports its constitutional powers, so it needs a specific bill with a clear purpose and scope and a major link to those powers.
Leaking the contents of an ongoing investigation could let suspects collude or flee, so, given separation of powers and prosecutors' independence, ongoing case files cannot be obtained.

Once a case is closed, there is no real obstruction of investigation, so files may be obtained by a full-chamber resolution; if disclosure could harm a related separate investigation, prosecutors may delay providing them. Copies identical to the originals also require a full-chamber resolution.

Files may contain state secrets, privacy and business secrets, so information must be used only as necessary for constitutional powers, with reputations and privacy protected, and without commenting on the handling of individual cases for unrelated purposes.
The Legislative Yuan's document power and the Control Yuan's investigation power differ in nature and purpose and do not overlap, so prosecutors cannot refuse on that ground.
Disputes should be settled by negotiation or by a law setting conditions and procedures, and the relevant bodies should quickly build a legal mechanism for resolving them.

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional for the authorities to cancel the residence certificate and original-household rights of military dependents' village residents who refuse to agree to rebuilding an old village. The court held that this cancellation does not violate the constitutional equality principle. It also said the rebuilding law has not fully weighed the situations of those who refuse, and that the relevant authorities should promptly review and improve it.
raw.held: Cancelling the residence certificate and original-household rights of households that do not agree to rebuilding does not conflict with the equality principle in Article 7 of the Constitution. However, the rebuilding law's balancing of interests is not yet appropriate, and the relevant authorities should promptly conduct an overall review and make improvements.

points.text: Equality means substantive equality, not mechanical sameness. Different treatment is allowed if its purpose is constitutional and the means have a reasonable link to that purpose.
The legislature has wide freedom to set how social benefits are distributed and may limit welfare resources, as long as the purpose is legitimate and the means reasonably connected to it.
The rule treats households that refuse differently from those that agree, because refusers cannot buy the new housing or receive the housing purchase subsidy.

The purpose is legitimate: avoiding delay and rising costs, encouraging residents to persuade one another, and using the land efficiently for the public interest. Housing allocation is a welfare measure in the nature of a loan for use, and ending it did not require the household's consent. All households had the same chance to agree and knew the consequence of refusing.

The law is nonetheless incomplete. Refusers also lose the relocation subsidy and demolition compensation that those who agree receive, and unlike unauthorized occupants who move on schedule they get no demolition compensation. The law also does not say how to treat the very few who refuse because they cannot afford the self-paid portion.

Some parts of the petitions were not accepted: they did not give concrete reasons, the petitioners were not parties to the judgment they challenged, or they did not explain how the rules violate the Constitution.

who: Original households of old military dependents' villages who refused rebuilding
Original households that agreed to rebuilding
Unauthorized occupants who moved on schedule
Households unable to afford the self-paid portion

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Economic Affairs rule requiring video arcades to follow local ordinances, and the Taipei, former Taipei County and Taoyuan County ordinances setting minimum distances (1,000, 990 and 800 meters) between arcades and places such as schools and hospitals, are constitutional. The court held that the rule and all three distance requirements are constitutional. It also urged local governments to review the distances regularly so they do not effectively shut arcades out.
raw.held: The rule requiring arcades to comply with local ordinances does not violate the legal reservation principle. The three local distance rules do not violate the division of central and local powers, the legal reservation principle or the proportionality principle, but local governments should review them as conditions change.

points.text: The Ministry's rule only says which laws apply when applying for an arcade grade certificate. It is a detailed, technical matter, so it does not breach the legal reservation principle.

Regulating arcades is a local self-government matter of commercial guidance and management. The central arcade law gives local authorities certain powers, so local ordinances that do not conflict with central rules are allowed under the constitution's division of powers.

The Local Government Act lets local governments limit residents' rights by ordinance within a reasonable scope. The central law's 50-meter distance is a minimum that leaves room for longer local distances, so the ordinances stay within that authorization.

The distance rules limit how a business is carried out (where it operates). They aim to protect social peace, public morals, public safety and public health, which is a legitimate aim, and they help achieve it.

Longer distances are a necessary means because they achieve the aim without costly close supervision of arcades near sensitive places, and the limit is reasonably balanced against the public interest, so it does not breach proportionality.
Distances well above the legal minimum could effectively block arcades and would then face stricter review. Local governments should therefore adjust the rules as conditions change.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Mass Rapid Transit Act and related rules may let authorities expropriate land next to metro facilities for development purposes, even when that land is not needed for the transit business itself. The Constitutional Court said that, to the extent they allow taking land that transit does not need, these rules violate the Constitution's proportionality principle and the protection of property and residence. They can no longer be applied from the day of the ruling.
raw.held: The provisions allowing expropriation of neighboring land for development, beyond land truly necessary for transit, are unconstitutional to that extent and are not to be applied from the date of the ruling. Some other parts of the petitions were dismissed as inadmissible.

points.text: Expropriation limits property rights and, where people lawfully live on the land, seriously affects their freedom of residence. It must serve a public use or other public interest and be necessary, and the owner must receive reasonable and prompt compensation.

Under the expropriation rules the ruling cites, land taken for transport must be what the transport business actually needs. The neighboring land the provisions cover is broad, so it is hard to say all of it is needed for transit.

The older 1988 provision and the development measures also let land be expropriated for joint development without defining its extent. This too may reach land transit does not need, burdening property and residence.

Taking land needed for transit is a public use. Developing neighboring land has a public-interest aim (using land well, promoting local growth, helping fund construction), but taking non-necessary land imposes a special sacrifice on owners and shifts the benefit to the state or private parties.

Less harmful alternatives exist, such as cooperative joint development with incentives, land readjustment, zone expropriation that returns equal-value land, or other gentler methods. Expropriating non-necessary land is therefore not necessary and not the least harmful means, so it fails the proportionality principle.

Other parts of the petitions were dismissed: some provisions were not applied in the final judgment, one was already made inapplicable by this ruling, and some complaints were not specifically argued.

who: Owners of land next to metro facilities
People lawfully living on such land
Petitioners whose challenges were dismissed in part

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Civil Associations Act is constitutional. The rule says a professional association's chair must be chosen by the directors, from among the standing directors or, if there are none, from among the directors. The court held that this rule limits the association's freedom to run its own internal affairs more than necessary, so it violates the Constitution.
raw.held: The rule requiring directors to elect the chair of a professional association is unconstitutional because it goes beyond what is necessary and conflicts with freedom of association. It loses effect one year after the ruling is announced, at the latest.

points.text: Freedom of association protects a group's right to decide its own internal organization and affairs, including how its representative or head is chosen. Limits must stay within what is necessary, and how much limit is allowed depends on the kind of group.

The rule is mandatory for professional associations, so it restricts their self-determination over internal organization and affairs. For social and political groups the rule can be changed by their bylaws, so it is not mandatory for them.
The rule aims to help civil associations develop soundly. A chair's duties, such as carrying out the association's work and calling meetings, affect internal operations and healthy development.

Whether the chair is chosen by directors, directly by members, or by another suitable method set in the bylaws, the association's aims are not harmed. Forcing election by directors therefore goes beyond what is necessary.
Special professional associations covered by other laws that restrict how their chair is chosen for other public-interest reasons are outside this ruling.

who: Chairs and directors of professional associations

raw.answer: The case asked whether a tax rule letting only joint practitioners, or those whose fees are collected and passed on by a professional association, choose accrual-basis accounting is unconstitutional. The court found that the rule leaves out some solo practitioners who are similar in situation, and so it conflicts with the constitutional principle of equality to that extent. Other challenges raised by the applicant were not accepted for review.
raw.held: The rule is inconsistent with the equality principle in Article 7 of the Constitution to the extent that it does not cover solo practitioners whose income and expenses span years, who run large operations, and whose accounting is complex like a company's.

points.text: Equality under Article 7 is tested by asking whether the purpose of the different treatment is constitutional and whether the classification is reasonably connected to that purpose.
The rule creates different treatment: only joint practitioners or those with association-collected fees can choose accrual accounting, while others use the cash basis.
The purpose is constitutional: joint practices resemble companies with complex accounting, and association-collected fees are often paid late across years, so choice of accrual accounting suits them.

The classification by business form and fee collection does not achieve that purpose, because solo practitioners may also be large, have complex accounts, or receive or pay money across years, while joint practices may be small and simple.
So leaving out such solo practitioners lacks a reasonable link to the purpose and conflicts with Article 7 to that extent.

The applicant's other challenges and the request to supplement an earlier interpretation were not accepted, since they only disputed how courts applied the law and the earlier interpretation was not unclear.

who: Solo practitioners with large, complex, cross-year finances
Practitioners whose fees are collected by professional associations

raw.answer: A cosmetics company put a sunscreen ad on a shopping website without first getting government approval, and was fined NT$30,000 under the Cosmetics Hygiene Management Act. The company challenged the rules requiring advance approval of cosmetics ads and the fines for skipping it. The court decided these rules go too far and violate free speech protections.
raw.held: The rule requiring cosmetics companies to get advance approval for ads, and the fine for breaking it, are unconstitutional because they restrict free speech more than necessary. They lose effect from the day the ruling is published.

points.text: Truthful, non-misleading commercial speech aimed at lawful transactions that helps consumers make sound economic choices is protected by the constitutional guarantee of free speech, and cosmetics ads are commercial expression.

Advance approval of cosmetics ads is a major interference with free speech and is generally unconstitutional. It could be justified only if it prevents direct, immediate and hard-to-reverse harm to life, body or health, is directly and absolutely necessary, and allows quick court relief.

The rules aim to prevent obscene, indecent or false and exaggerated ads, but cosmetics are ordinary daily-use items and ads merely encourage buying, so they pose no direct, immediate threat to life or health. The aim is therefore not a especially important public interest, and no direct and absolutely necessary link to it exists.

Medicated cosmetics (such as sunscreen) affect health more, but their ads still pose no direct threat. Such products already need government approval and licensing, must carry required labels, and are covered by inspection rules and penalties, and false ads can already be punished.
So the rules fail the proportionality principle in Article 23 and conflict with the free speech guarantee in Article 11 of the Constitution.

The company's other challenges, to Article 24 paragraph 1 of the Act and to Article 20 of its enforcement rules, were not accepted because they did not specifically show how those rules violate the Constitution.

who: Health authorities that review cosmetics ads

raw.answer: Six people who paid inheritance and gift taxes late were charged late-payment fees (滯納金) and then interest on top, and they challenged these charges as unconstitutional. The court held that the late fees themselves and two Ministry of Finance letters about charging them are constitutional, but that charging interest on the late fees is unconstitutional.
raw.held: Late-payment fees under the Tax Collection Act art. 20 and the Estate and Gift Tax Act art. 51(1) are not unconstitutional, and the two Ministry of Finance letters do not violate the principle that taxes must rest on law. Interest on the unpaid tax is allowed, but interest charged on the late fees is invalid from the date of the ruling.

points.text: Late fees serve the legitimate aims of urging timely payment and making up for the state's revenue loss, so their purpose is proper.

Late fees help reach that aim, and people who truly cannot pay on time can seek extensions, installments or payment in kind to avoid them, so the fees are not clearly excessive and do not breach proportionality.
The authorities should still review whether the fee rate (1% per 2 days) is too high or its intervals too short, and whether the law should allow fees to be reduced or waived in individual cases.

The two letters only interpret existing law and do not touch the elements of a tax such as taxpayer, tax base or rate, and they match the purpose of the statutes, so they do not violate the principle of taxation by law.
Where a taxpayer appeals but pays half of the supplementary tax late, enforcement is no longer put on hold, so there is a need to urge payment and a fee on that half is proper.

Interest on unpaid tax compensates for delay and is allowed, but interest on late fees double-counts the delay loss, since the fee already acts partly as delay interest, and so is unreasonable and violates proportionality.

who: Taxpayers who pay inheritance or gift tax late
Taxpayers who appeal a review decision and pay the supplementary tax late

raw.answer: A person challenged a rule in the Ancestor Worship Associations Act saying that, for associations that existed before the Act, members (派下員) are decided by each association's own rules. Those rules mostly limit membership to male descendants, so most women are excluded. The court held that this rule is not contrary to the constitutional guarantee of gender equality and does not violate women's property rights, but it said the authorities should review the system over time.
raw.held: The rule that members of pre-existing ancestor worship associations are determined by their own rules is not found to conflict with Article 7 of the Constitution on gender equality or to infringe women's property rights.

points.text: The court treated the challenge as aimed at the statutory rule, since the final judgment relied on that rule, even though the association's own charter cannot itself be reviewed.
The rule does not use gender as its standard, and its aim is to keep the legal order stable and respect the principle that laws are not retroactive.

The association rules are private acts of association and property disposition by founders and descendants, protected by freedom of association, property rights, contract freedom and private autonomy, so they are generally respected.
Although the rules often exclude women and create unequal treatment in effect, it is not arbitrary, so it is not found to violate gender equality or infringe women's property rights.
The court noted that the fallback provision, used when there are no rules, does use gender, and unequal treatment remains in the overall system despite some softening provisions.

Because the Constitution's Additional Articles require the state to promote substantive gender equality, the relevant authorities should review and revise the rules in good time, balancing legal stability and the freedoms of association, property and contract.

who: Women excluded as members of pre-existing ancestor worship associations
Male-line descendants and adopted sons of founders
Founders' descendants who run these associations

raw.answer: Two petitioners challenged how Taiwan's income tax law treats salary income: it allows only a fixed deduction and no deduction of actual necessary expenses. A university teacher also argued that his part-time teaching fees should count as professional-practice income rather than salary. The court held that the fixed-only rule violates the equal protection clause to the extent it bars deducting necessary expenses that exceed the fixed amount, but that treating part-time university teaching fees as salary income is constitutional.
raw.held: The salary-income rules are inconsistent with the Constitution's equality guarantee (Article 7) to the extent they do not let salary earners deduct necessary expenses above the statutory deduction, and the relevant authorities must review and amend the law within two years. The Ministry of Finance's interpretation that part-time university teachers' lecture fees are salary income does not violate the principles of taxation by law (Article 19) or Article 23.

points.text: Professional-practice income and salary income are both earnings from labor and are similar in nature, yet the law lets professional-practice earners deduct actual costs and necessary expenses while salary earners get only a single fixed deduction. This creates unequal treatment between those groups and among salary earners.
The fixed deduction has a proper purpose: it eases the tax burden on salary earners and lowers collection costs, given the very large number of salary filers.

Under the ability-to-pay principle, tax should be based on net income after costs and necessary expenses. The fixed deduction is too simple because it ignores differences among salary earners and disadvantages those whose work requires clearly higher necessary expenses. It also is not necessarily tied to whether a person works independently. So the means lacks a reasonable connection to its purpose and conflicts with Article 7 to that extent.

A competent authority may interpret tax law within its powers if it follows constitutional principles, the legislative intent and ordinary interpretive methods. The Ministry's interpretation that part-time university teaching fees are salary income meets this standard, fits the legislative intent, helps clarify application, and adds no tax obligation the law does not provide.

The court also pointed out that authorities should comprehensively review how different incomes are classified and calculated, and whether deductible costs, expense standards and tax incentives are too generous.

who: Salary earners with necessary expenses above the fixed deduction

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's conflict-of-interest law is unconstitutional when it bars public officials and their related persons from trading with the agency the official serves or supervises, and fines violators one to three times the deal amount. The court held that the ban itself is constitutional, but that the fine rule is too harsh in some cases because it has no adjustment mechanism. The fine rule will lose effect within one year.
raw.held: The ban on trading (Article 9) does not violate the Constitution, though the authorities should promptly review its application to officials' related persons. The fine of one to three times the transaction amount (Article 15) violates the proportionality principle and the protection of property, and will lose effect no later than one year after the ruling is announced.

points.text: The ban and the fine limit work, property, business freedom and freedom of contract, which the Constitution protects, so any limit must meet the proportionality principle.
The purpose is legitimate: to stop unfair competition, improper transfer of benefits and conflicts of interest, and the ban and fine help achieve it.
The ban is necessary because without it officials could use their power to channel benefits, and no less harmful means would work as well.
The ban is not excessive, because it covers only the official's own agency or supervised agencies, so those affected can still trade with others.

Where banning related persons would leave only a few bidders and create a monopoly, harming the public interest, the authorities should review whether the ban is still needed when open and fair procedures exist; officials are held to a higher standard than related persons.
The fine is too harsh in some cases: the deal amount is often far higher than the profit, and even the minimum of one times the amount may be unaffordable, yet the law has no adjustment mechanism.

who: Relatives and other related persons of public officials
Government agencies that make purchases, leases or contracts

raw.answer: The case asked whether a law letting authorities announce which acts count as polluting the environment was valid, and whether Tainan City's announcement banning unapproved advertisements in certain places went too far. The court held the law itself is acceptable, but Tainan's announcement went beyond what the law allowed because it treated every unapproved advertisement as pollution. The announcement loses effect within three months of the ruling.
raw.held: The provision of the Waste Disposal Act allowing authorities to announce other polluting acts does not violate the constitutional requirement that a law's delegation be clear. Tainan's announcements exceeded that delegation and lose effect no later than three months after the ruling is published.

points.text: Limits on people's basic rights should generally be set by law; authorities may fill in details only if the law clearly states the purpose, content and scope of the delegation, and the rules they issue must stay within it.

Read as a whole, the Waste Disposal Act's purposes (clearing waste, improving environmental sanitation, protecting public health) and its listed acts show the delegation is clear enough, so announced acts must be comparable in polluting effect to the ten listed ones.
Other listed provisions show that polluting the environment is not limited to dumping waste; other acts harming sanitation and public health can count too.

Tainan's announcement banned and punished unapproved advertisements in listed places and ways, without asking whether they harm sanitation or health or reach a comparable level of pollution, so it went beyond the law's authorization.
The authority must promptly revise its rules so that only unapproved advertising reaching the required level of pollution is a violation; the announcement loses effect within three months.
Because advertising is a form of expression protected by free speech, the authority must consider the necessity and appropriateness of any resulting limits on speech or other rights when revising.
Parts of the petition were not accepted: complaints about how a court applied the law, and about a separate announcement not applied in the final judgment.

who: People who put up advertisements in Tainan City

raw.answer: A person whose urban renewal case ended in a final court ruling asked the court to clarify its earlier Interpretation No. 725. That ruling said that when a law is declared invalid after a set period, the person who requested the interpretation can seek a retrial or other relief in their own case. The court decided that this applies to every person who obtained such a delayed-invalidity interpretation, including those before No. 725, and that the Prosecutor General can also act.
raw.held: Everyone who asked for an interpretation in which the court declared the law applied in their final ruling invalid after a set period can seek a retrial or other relief in their original case, and the Prosecutor General can file an extraordinary appeal. This covers interpretations issued before No. 725, and No. 725 is supplemented accordingly.

points.text: The request for clarification was accepted because No. 725 did not say who counts as the person whose case qualifies, and the applicant's final ruling relied on it.
Earlier interpretations (Nos. 177 and 185) allowed retrial or extraordinary appeal in the original case but did not say whether this applies when invalidity is delayed, so No. 725 supplemented them.
Individual relief protects the applicant and recognizes their contribution to upholding the constitution, whether the law becomes invalid immediately or after a delay.

No. 725's wording refers to any interpretation declaring a law invalid after a set period, and it is a system-wide rule, so it covers all such interpretations, including earlier ones, not only its own applicant.
Courts must still check whether each case meets the deadlines and other procedural rules for retrial and whether it has merit.
The part of the request about Interpretation No. 709 was not accepted because the applicant did not specify what was unclear or poorly reasoned.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Teachers' Act is unconstitutional in letting schools dismiss, suspend or not renew teachers for misconduct that harms the dignity of the teaching profession, and in barring such people from being hired. The court held that the misconduct standard is clear enough and that dismissing already-hired teachers is constitutional. It struck down the lifetime ban on being hired as a teacher.
raw.held: The standard of misconduct harming the teaching profession, and dismissal, suspension or non-renewal of hired teachers with approval from the education authority, were held constitutional. The rule barring such people from being hired as teachers violates the proportionality principle and loses effect when one year has passed from the ruling's announcement, unless revised sooner.

points.text: The misconduct standard is an open-ended concept, but it is not too vague. Its meaning can be understood, teachers can foresee it from training, codes and past cases such as sexual harassment, severe corporal punishment, exam cheating and plagiarism, and courts can review it.
Both the hiring bar and dismissal limit the freedom to choose an occupation by a personal qualification. They therefore need an important public interest and a necessary means.

Protecting students' right to education and the constitutional educational goals is an important public interest, and stricter treatment of teachers whose misconduct harms the profession helps serve it.

Dismissal, suspension or non-renewal is not excessive. The misconduct must be serious enough to harm the profession, lesser conduct gets milder responses, and no gentler measure achieves the same aim.
The lifetime ban on re-employment removes any chance to reform. It sets no waiting period or conditions for people who can show they have changed, so it goes beyond what is necessary.
The authorities must review and revise the hiring bar within one year of the ruling, or that part loses effect.

who: Teachers dismissed, suspended or not renewed for misconduct
People barred from being hired as teachers

raw.answer: The case challenged Taiwan's Urban Renewal Act, under which owners can apply to government to carry out urban renewal projects that can affect other owners' property and homes. The court found that the procedures for approving a project outline and a project plan, and the low consent threshold for applying for outline approval, did not meet constitutional due process. It upheld the higher consent thresholds for approving project plans and a special rule for disaster areas.
raw.held: The rules on approving renewal outlines and plans, and the one-tenth consent threshold for outline applications, are unconstitutional because they fail due process and harm property and residence rights; the authorities must fix them within one year or those parts lose effect. The consent thresholds for plan approval and the disaster-area rule (limited to its stated conditions) were held constitutional.

points.text: Property rights and the freedom of residence can be limited by law only for the public good and within the proportionality principle.
Approving a renewal outline or plan is an administrative act that limits property and residence rights, and can even lead to loss of rights and forced moves.

Due process requires a fair, professional and diverse review body, ways for interested people to learn the information and state their views, and for plan approval a public hearing with reasons given for accepting or rejecting views.
The outline approval rules set up no proper review body and did not ensure interested people could learn the information; a public meeting was not enough to let them state views.
A consent threshold of just over one-tenth for applying for outline approval is too low, lets a small minority force the majority into the process, and fails due process.
The plan approval rules did not require individual delivery of information to other owners or a public hearing, so they fail due process.

The plan-approval consent thresholds (all over one-half) serve legitimate aims and are proportionate, though they should be reviewed; the disaster-area rule is proportionate only within its stated limits.

who: Owners of land and lawful buildings in renewal areas

raw.answer: A suspect and her defense lawyer asked to see the prosecutor's file when the prosecutor asked a court to detain her during an investigation, and were refused. The court held that under the Constitution's due process principle, suspects and their lawyers must be told the reasons for the detention request and, with limited exceptions, shown the related evidence. The current law, which only tells them the facts behind the grounds for detention, falls short.
raw.held: The current rules, which only tell a suspect and lawyer the facts behind the grounds for detention, do not meet constitutional due process. The authorities must amend the law within one year; if they do not, courts must follow this ruling when reviewing detention during investigations.

points.text: The court could review Article 101(3) as well as Article 33(1), because the real question was how suspects and lawyers learn the grounds and evidence for a detention request, and evaluating that required both provisions.
Personal liberty and the right to sue are protected by Articles 8 and 16, so depriving someone of liberty requires due process. Detention seriously harms a person, so it should be used carefully.

The reasons and evidence in a detention request are what the judge relies on to take away liberty. So the suspect and lawyer must be told in a suitable way and in time to defend effectively, though access may be limited where there is a risk of destroying or tampering with evidence, colluding, or endangering others.
Read together, the two provisions give suspects and lawyers only the facts behind the grounds for detention, not the specific reasons or the evidence, which does not match due process.
How to disclose is left to the legislature (file review, the judge showing or telling, or another method), but any method must meet due process.
Secrecy of investigations should not block due process, since the exceptions already balance the interests. Equal-arms principles do not apply because the current law has no adversarial structure.

who: Criminal suspects facing a detention request

raw.answer: A company that had to withhold tax from payments was penalized for not reporting withholding statements on time, even though it had already paid the missing tax before the deadline. A Ministry of Finance rule fined such a person 1.5 times the unpaid or underwithheld tax. The court held that the fine amount went further than necessary and violated the Constitution, so the rule can no longer be applied.
raw.held: The fine amount in the Ministry of Finance rule (1.5 times the tax not withheld or underwithheld, where the tax was paid in time but the statement was reported late) exceeds what is necessary. It violates the proportionality principle and property rights, and it stops being applied from the day the interpretation was announced.

points.text: The court accepted the rule for review because the final court judgment relied on it in substance, even though the judgment did not name it.
Failing to withhold tax and failing to file withholding statements harm tax revenue and the public interest to clearly different degrees.
A person who paid the tax in time but only reported the statements late causes less harm than one who did not pay, yet the rule treated both the same with a flat 1.5 times fine.

The rule gave tax authorities no room to set the fine according to how serious the violation was, so the penalty went beyond what is necessary and breaches the proportionality principle and property rights.
The court noted that the relevant authorities should consider each case's seriousness and make suitable, proportionate arrangements under Article 48-3 of the Tax Collection Act.

The separate request about the Income Tax Act's definition of Republic of China source income was not accepted, as it did not show a constitutional conflict and merely disputed how the court applied the law.

who: Withholding agents who paid tax late-reported statements
Applicant who challenged the Income Tax Act provision

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 48 of Taiwan's Soil and Groundwater Pollution Remediation Act is unconstitutional. The article makes people who caused pollution before the Act took effect responsible for cleaning up pollution that still exists after it took effect. The court decided the rule is not unconstitutional.
raw.held: The part of Article 48 applying the cleanup duties to polluters whose pollution began before the Act took effect governs only pollution that still exists after the Act took effect. It does not violate the principle against retroactive laws or the proportionality principle in Article 23 of the Constitution, and it does not violate the protection of work and property rights in Article 15.

points.text: The rule is not retroactive. The cleanup duty targets pollution that still exists, whether the polluting act happened before or after the Act. If pollution ended before the Act and none remains, the rule does not apply.
Pre-Act polluters have no protected expectation that would require transition provisions or other remedies, because their pollution came from illegal acts.
The duties limit work, property and business freedom, so they must pass the proportionality principle in Article 23 of the Constitution.
The purpose is legitimate: cleaning up soil and groundwater, protecting health and the environment, and handling old pollution that persists. The means help achieve that purpose.

The means are necessary. Without making these polluters responsible, others or the state would bear the harm, which is unjust and burdens public finances, and no less harmful means would work as well.
The burden on polluters is not clearly out of balance with the public interest, since lingering pollution harms health and the environment and the polluting acts were illegal.
The rule covers only the polluters themselves. Whether their general successors inherit the cleanup duty is outside the rule, so the equality question raised does not arise.

who: Polluters whose pollution began before the Act
Businesses in farming, industry and commerce

raw.answer: Two people challenged changes made to city plans during the periodic comprehensive review, and asked the court to supplement an earlier interpretation (No. 156). The court held that such a review change is a rule-like measure, not an administrative disposition. But if a specific item directly restricts the rights of particular people, or of a identifiable group, or adds to their burdens, they may file an administrative appeal or lawsuit over that item. It also told the legislature to add rules within two years so people can sue over unlawful city plans.
