raw.held: A periodic-review change to a city plan is a rule, not an administrative disposition, but people directly restricted or burdened by a specific item may appeal or sue over that part. The legislature must add rules for suing over unlawful city plans within two years; after that, existing appeal and court rules for unlawful administrative dispositions apply to plans issued.

points.text: The court accepted the request to supplement the earlier interpretation, since the final court judgments relied on it and the applicants had proper grounds for doubt.
The Constitution protects property rights and the right to sue; where rights are harmed, people must have a chance to seek timely and effective court relief.

The law does not clearly limit what a periodic review may change, so whether an item directly restricts or burdens specific people varies. Appeal bodies and administrative courts must examine each item's content to decide whether it is a case-specific change that counts as an administrative disposition and can be challenged.

Because city plans are rules, people currently must wait for a later administrative disposition before suing. Yet plans heavily affect land use and are hard to separate from dispositions, so the legislature must add rules within two years allowing suits over unlawful plans, failing which the rules for unlawful administrative dispositions apply by analogy to plans issued after two years.
Whether one applicant's specific remark in a Taipei review notice has that effect is for the administrative courts to decide, so that part of the request was not accepted.

who: Landowners in areas affected by city plan changes
People directly restricted or burdened by specific plan items

raw.answer: A temple and its development company said a national highway tunnel ran under their land without their consent, and the highway bureau refused to buy or expropriate rights to the land. The court decided that when a project passes over or under private land and goes beyond what an owner should have to tolerate, the owner may ask the project's land user to apply to the authority for expropriation of an underground or aerial use right (地上權). It found the Land Expropriation Act lacks such a rule and told the authorities to fix this.
raw.held: An owner may ask the land-needing party to apply to the authority to expropriate a surface-right (地上權) when a project crosses above or below the land beyond the owner's social responsibility to tolerate and imposes a special sacrifice. The relevant agencies must amend the Act within one year of the ruling; if they do not, owners may make this request directly based on the ruling.

points.text: The constitutional protection of property covers more than outright seizure; if public power causes losses beyond what owners should tolerate, a special sacrifice, the state must give reasonable compensation.

When a facility already crosses private land above or below and exceeds what the owner should tolerate without compensation, the owner's property has already been harmed, so the owner must be given the right to actively request expropriation.
Article 11 (the first provision) only covers the price-negotiation steps before expropriation and does not say whether owners can ask for expropriation.

Article 57, paragraph 2 applies only when land cannot be put to reasonable use and covers ownership, not a surface right; Article 57, paragraph 1 lets the land user get a surface right but gives owners no right to request expropriation. Together they fall short of the constitutional purpose.

For legal certainty, owners must use this right within a set time, which the legislature must set within reasonable limits, and the current one-year period in Article 57, paragraph 2 should be reviewed.

The petitioners may make the request within three months of the ruling being delivered, but whether their land is actually crossed and the sacrifice exceeds the tolerable limit is a factual question outside this ruling.

who: Private landowners whose land is crossed above or below by public projects
Entities that need land for public projects
The petitioners (the temple and its development company)
Legislators and agencies amending the Act

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's law on mainland Chinese people was constitutional where it let authorities deport them without letting them respond, and where it let them be held in custody before deportation without clear reasons or a time limit. The court held that these parts violated the Constitution, and that the deportation rules on the meaning of entering without permission were acceptable. It also held that the custody reasons set in an administrative regulation lacked a clear legal basis.
raw.held: The court held that deporting mainland people who entered lawfully, without giving them a chance to respond (except in urgent security or public-order cases), is unconstitutional. It also held that the temporary detention rules lacked clear grounds, prompt court remedy, court review and a time limit, and that the regulation's detention grounds lacked clear legal authorization. These parts lose effect within two years of the ruling unless fixed. Two implementing rules on entry without permission were held not to go beyond the statute.

points.text: Lawfully admitted mainland people are in principle protected by freedom of movement, so forcing them out requires fair procedure unless urgent action is needed for national security or public order. The law gave no chance to respond.

Detention before deportation takes away personal liberty, so its grounds must be set clearly by law. The statute's wording was too broad and did not limit detention to cases where deportation would otherwise be very difficult, which breaches the clarity principle.

Short temporary detention during a reasonable deportation process need not be ordered by a court, but the detained person must have prompt judicial remedy. Detention must go to a court within 24 hours if the person objects, and continued detention after the temporary period needs a court order.
The statute sets no time limit on detention, which does not serve the aim of quick deportation and risks excessive deprivation of liberty, breaching proportionality.

The implementing rules on what counts as entering without permission, and on interview findings of sham marriage, stay within the statute's meaning and so do not violate the legal reservation principle.

The deportation-handling regulation listed detention grounds, but the statute only authorized rules on deportation procedure and detention facilities, not on detention grounds. So it lacked clear legal authorization.

who: Mainland Chinese people lawfully admitted to Taiwan
People held in temporary detention before deportation

raw.answer: The case asked whether an employer and worker who agree on special working hours, rest days, holidays or women's night work still have to follow the Labor Standards Act's limits if the agreement was never filed for approval with the local authority. The court held that the filing requirement is mandatory, so an unfiled agreement cannot override those limits. It did not, however, declare such an agreement void.
raw.held: The filing requirement in Article 84-1 of the Labor Standards Act is mandatory. An agreement that was not filed cannot set aside the limits in Articles 30, 32, 36, 37 and 49. Besides causing public-law disadvantages for the employer, courts hearing a dispute must adjust the terms to those articles and calculate pay under Articles 24 and 39.

points.text: Two top courts, the Supreme Court and the Supreme Administrative Court, disagreed about whether an unfiled agreement still has effect, which is why a ruling was needed.

The Constitution protects workers, and the Act sets minimum working conditions. Working time, rest days, holidays and women's night work strongly affect workers' health and welfare, so parties cannot avoid these minimums by invoking freedom of contract unless the Act makes an exception.

The central-authority announcement and local filing requirements exist to protect workers and prevent arbitrary or excessive use of special agreements, so whether an unfiled agreement has civil effect must be judged by those aims.

Filing is more than an administrative formality. Longer hours affect health, the same work can differ by region so local authorities need to check each case, and workers are usually the weaker party in bargaining. The filing requirement is therefore a mandatory rule under Civil Code Article 71.

An unfiled agreement is not automatically void, because such agreements are complex and mix terms favorable and unfavorable to workers. Without filing, though, it cannot displace the Act's limits, so courts adjust it case by case and set pay under the Act.

The request to unify interpretation of the Supreme Court judgment against Interpretation No. 494 was not accepted, because court views that differ from the Constitutional Court's interpretations must yield to those interpretations.

who: Employers and workers with special working-hour agreements
Workers in specially designated job types

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is constitutional to require landowners to apply for "offset land" (land returned in place of cash compensation) within the public notice period when the written notice reaches them after the notice date. The court held that counting the period from the notice date in that situation does not meet the constitutional requirement of fair administrative procedure and violates the protection of property rights in Article 15. The rule must be reviewed and revised within one year.
raw.held: Where the written notice of a zone expropriation is delivered after the public notice date, the rule that still counts the application period from the public notice date is unconstitutional. The authorities must review and revise it within one year, or that part loses effect.

points.text: Property rights are protected by Article 15. The state may expropriate land for public purposes but must give reasonable and appropriate compensation promptly.

Offset land is a form of expropriation compensation, and its application deadline limits property rights. So it needs fair administrative procedure, including making sure affected people get the information in time to assert their rights.
The law requires both a public notice and a written notice to owners, so that they learn the relevant information and can exercise their rights, including seeking remedies if needed.

Owners may choose between cash and offset land. If the written notice arrives after the public notice date but the 30 days still run from the public notice date, owners cannot be sure of getting the information they need to choose, or of having the full 30 days.

The court also pointed out that authorities should state the estimated offset-land unit price in the notices, and should review whether the application period should be extended when an owner objects to the compensation amount.

who: Local and city/county authorities handling expropriation
Owners who prefer offset land over cash compensation

raw.answer: The case asked how a detained defendant in Taiwan can go to court when unhappy with a decision on their complaint about how the detention center treated them. The court said that until the detention rules are amended, such a defendant may seek relief from the court that ordered the detention, using the rules on a challenge to a court order (準抗告) in the Code of Criminal Procedure. This adds to an earlier ruling, Interpretation No. 653.
raw.held: Until the relevant rules are amended and promulgated, a detained defendant who disagrees with an authority's decision on their complaint may ask the court that ordered the detention for relief, using the Code of Criminal Procedure article 416 rules on challenges to court orders. Interpretation No. 653 is supplemented accordingly.

points.text: Detention seriously interferes with personal liberty, so a detainee who says the detaining authority's adverse decision went beyond what was needed for the detention's purpose or the order of the facility, and unlawfully harmed constitutional rights, should be able to seek court relief.

Interpretation No. 653 already found that the provisions barring detainees from suing in court conflict with the constitutional protection of the right to bring lawsuits, and told the authorities to revise the rules within two years.
That two-year period expired long ago and the rules were still not amended.

To protect the litigation rights of detainees unhappy with the treatment or measures of the detention center, the court allows court relief in the meantime through the challenge-to-court-order rules, before the court that ordered detention.
The petitioner may seek relief over the isolation measure and the complaint decision in the underlying case within five days after this interpretation is served.

who: The petitioner in the underlying case

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the implementing regulations of the School Staff Retirement Act is unconstitutional. The rule capped the combined retirement pay of school staff who retired, then returned to work at a public school and retired again, counting their earlier retirement together with the new one. The court held the rule unconstitutional because no law clearly authorized it, and it will lose effect within one year unless it is fixed sooner.
raw.held: Article 19, paragraph 2 of the implementing regulations is unconstitutional because it lacks specific legal authorization and adds a limit the law does not contain. It violates the property right in Article 15 and the legal-reservation principle in Article 23, and it loses effect no later than one year after the ruling is published.

points.text: The right of public school staff to claim retirement pay under the Act is a constitutionally protected property right. Limiting it requires a law or a specific, clear authorization from the legislature.

The Act's provisions on pension base amounts, the 35-year maximum, and combining service before and after the Act's amendment do not say whether service after re-employment must be combined with earlier retirement service up to a maximum.
Article 14 of the Act only treats pre-retirement service and re-employment service as counted separately, and it sets no combined ceiling.
The regulations rest only on the Act's general authorization clause, and the Act as a whole does not show the legislature meant to let the agency set this rule by regulation.
The rule therefore adds a limit the law does not contain on the retirement pay claim. This infringes the property right and breaches the legal-reservation principle.

Designing a system for re-retirement involves many factors, such as how to count service, fairness, and state finances. The relevant agencies must review and amend the law within one year, and if they do not, the rule lapses.

who: Public school staff who retired and later returned to work at a public school
Public school staff who moved to a public school after receiving retirement or severance pay
Agencies responsible for amending the retirement law and rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 33 of the Teachers' Act is unconstitutional, and whether teachers can sue in court when school measures harm their rights or legal interests. The court said teachers can seek court relief under the administrative or civil litigation rules. It also found Article 33 is not unconstitutional.
raw.held: Teachers who believe a specific school measure has harmed their rights or legal interests may seek relief in court under the administrative or civil litigation rules. Article 33 of the Teachers' Act only sets out relief routes, does not limit public school teachers' right to bring administrative suits, and does not conflict with Article 16 of the Constitution.

points.text: Article 16 of the Constitution protects the right to sue, meaning a person whose rights or legal interests are harmed can ask a court for relief, and this cannot be restricted just because of someone's status or occupation.
Article 33 of the Teachers' Act only states the routes of relief for teachers and does not limit public school teachers' right to file administrative suits, so it does not violate Article 16.

Teachers harmed by specific school measures (such as absence records, pay deductions, year-end evaluations keeping the original salary, or teacher assessments) may go to court like ordinary people, consistent with the principle that a right comes with a remedy.
Courts hearing such cases should give appropriate respect to schools' professional judgments and their familiarity with the facts.

The request to change or supplement Interpretation No. 382 was not accepted, because that interpretation concerned remedies for students and the cited judgment did not apply it to measures against teachers.

The challenge to the vague wording and review procedure of a university's teacher assessment rules was not accepted, because the applicant did not concretely show how they conflict with the Constitution.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a person whose petition led the court to declare a law unconstitutional, with the law set to expire on a later date, can get relief in their own underlying case during that waiting period. The court said yes: the petitioner can seek a retrial or other relief, and courts cannot refuse just because the law stays valid until the deadline. The ruling also supplements two earlier interpretations and stops one administrative court precedent from being used.
raw.held: When the court declares a law applied in a final judgment unconstitutional but lets it expire later, the petitioner can seek retrial or other relief in the underlying case, and the Prosecutor General can file an extraordinary appeal. Courts may not reject these on the ground that the law is still valid until the deadline; if the ruling does not set a specific remedy, the case is decided under the new law once it takes effect.

points.text: Delayed expiry is meant to respect the lawmaking authority of other bodies and avoid a legal vacuum or sudden shock, and it does not change the fact that the law was declared unconstitutional.

Earlier interpretations Nos. 177 and 185 already let petitioners seek retrial or extraordinary appeal when a law was struck down with immediate effect, but they did not say what happens when expiry is delayed, so a supplement was needed.

To carry out those earlier interpretations, petitioners in delayed-expiry cases should likewise get retrial or other relief, and courts cannot reject it because the law remains valid until the deadline.
For real relief, the court's own specified remedy applies if it gives one; otherwise the case is decided under the new law after it takes effect.
An administrative court precedent (No. 615 of 1997) that denied retroactive effect where the law stays valid for a period conflicts with this ruling and is no longer to be applied.

Article 273, paragraph 2 of the Administrative Procedure Act, allowing a retrial suit, does not exclude laws declared unconstitutional with delayed expiry, so it is consistent with the ruling and not unconstitutional.

who: Petitioners whose petitions led to the ruling

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is constitutional for Taiwan's immigration agency to detain foreigners awaiting deportation without giving them quick access to a court, and to keep detaining them past a short period without a court deciding. The court held that the detention rules were unconstitutional in two respects: no prompt court review for short-term detention, and no court decision for detention beyond that short period. The rules lose effect after two years unless the law is fixed.
raw.held: The detention provision in the immigration law is contrary to the constitutional protection of personal liberty because it gives no prompt court remedy during temporary detention and lets the agency, not a court, decide on longer detention. It will lose effect no later than two years after the ruling is published.

points.text: Personal liberty is a basic human right protected by Article 8 of the Constitution, and it covers foreigners as well as citizens.
Detaining foreigners for removal is a serious restriction of liberty, so it needs court procedures or other due process, though not necessarily the same as for criminal defendants.

A short temporary detention by the agency, to carry out deportation arrangements, is reasonable and needs no court order, but the detainee must get prompt court review (transfer to a court within 24 hours if they object or ask) and be told of reasons and remedies in a language they understand. The temporary period may not exceed 15 days.
Detention beyond the temporary period deprives liberty for a long time, so an impartial, independent court must decide, with the agency applying to court before the period ends.
The law lacks prompt, effective court relief for temporary detention, and lets the agency alone order longer detention, so it violates due process and Article 8.
Because fixing the law needs time and a complete set of supporting rules, the authorities have two years to revise it; otherwise the unconstitutional part loses effect.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a no-confidence motion against the Premier can be brought in a special session of the Legislative Yuan that was called for other specific matters. The court decided that it can, because the Constitution does not forbid it. A provision of the Legislative Yuan's organizational law that limits special sessions to the matters set for them no longer applies to the extent it conflicts with this.
raw.held: Considering a no-confidence motion in a special session is not forbidden by the Constitution. The part of Article 6(1) of the Legislative Yuan Organization Act that limits special sessions to their specified matters, where it conflicts with this, is no longer applied. If a motion is filed while the Legislative Yuan is in recess, it must promptly convene a special session to consider it.

points.text: The constitutional provision on no-confidence motions only sets a deadline: the vote must be held by roll call within 48 hours, starting 72 hours after the motion is filed. This avoids prolonged uncertainty harming political stability. It does not require the motion to be filed in a regular session.
Article 69 of the Constitution only governs how a special session is convened, not which matters it may consider.
Because the Constitution requires no-confidence motions to be handled quickly, considering one in a special session is not forbidden.

The organizational law's limit of special sessions to their specified matters does not allow a no-confidence motion in a session called for other matters, so it conflicts with the Constitution and no longer applies to that extent.
Since the Constitution sets no time limit for filing the motion, a motion filed during recess requires the Legislative Yuan to convene a special session at once.
Procedural rules on filing and reviewing motions are the Legislative Yuan's own internal matter, but they must still respect the 72-hour and 48-hour voting timeline.

who: The Legislative Yuan as an institution

raw.answer: The case asked whether Ministry of Finance orders on how much of a land donation an individual can deduct on their income tax were constitutional. The orders let the deduction be set by standards the Ministry approved, or at 16% of the officially announced current land value. The court held that this did not meet the constitutional principle that taxes must be set by law, so the orders can no longer be applied.
raw.held: The parts of the six Ministry of Finance orders (2003 to 2008) that set the donated-land deduction by Ministry-approved standards, by case-by-case Ministry approval for special non-reserved land, or at 16% of announced current land value, violate Article 19 of the Constitution. They may not be applied from the day the ruling is announced.

points.text: Article 19 means the key elements of a tax, including the tax base, or any tax relief, must be set by law or by a regulation the law clearly authorizes. Administrative agencies may only make rules on minor detail or technical matters.
The Income Tax Act allows deductions for donations, but it does not say how to value donated goods such as land, and it does not clearly authorize the authority to set that by order.

The six orders only gave general rules or fixed a standard: the first two left it to Ministry-approved standards, and the later ones set 16% of announced current land value, with case-by-case approval for special cases.
Such orders are administrative rules, which may cover only minor details and technical matters.

How the deduction amount is calculated relates to the tax base and affects the amount a person can deduct. It is therefore a significant matter affecting taxes owed and property rights, not a minor detail, and must be set by law or a clearly authorized regulation.

who: Individuals who donate land and claim an income tax deduction

raw.answer: Several taxi drivers had been convicted of certain crimes, and as a result their taxi registration was revoked and their driver's licenses were revoked. They argued the traffic law was unconstitutional. The court found that banning drivers from taxi work based only on the crime and sentence went too far, and that revoking their driver's licenses went too far as well.
raw.held: The rule on suspending and revoking taxi registration must be fixed within two years or that part lapses, and until then a driver whose registration is revoked cannot re-register for three years. The part revoking driver's licenses lost effect immediately, and the related three-year bar on re-taking a license lapsed with it.

points.text: Protecting passenger safety and public order is an important public interest, so the aim of limiting who may be a taxi driver is constitutional.

A limit on who may work as a taxi driver is acceptable only if it targets people who pose a real risk to passengers, but the rule is based mainly on crime categories, which include offenses unrelated to passenger safety.
The government's data did not show that people who committed these crimes would reuse their taxi work to endanger passengers within a set period.

The rule applies the same ban whether the court gave a short sentence or a suspended one, without asking whether the conduct shows real risk to passengers, so it goes beyond what is necessary and violates the right to work.

Revoking the taxi registration already achieves the safety goal, so also revoking the driver's license takes away the freedom to drive and goes too far; the related three-year bar on re-taking a license falls with it.
Because drivers could otherwise keep or regain professional licenses and re-register at once, the court set a temporary three-year bar on re-registration to preserve the intended ban.

who: Taxi drivers convicted of the listed crimes
Drivers whose licenses were revoked under the rule
Government agencies that must amend the law
